parole.significato: used to form past passive participles from verbs in -ити (-yty) and -ати (-aty), which are frequently lexicalized into…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -еньнъ (-enĭnŭ), from енъ (enŭ) + -ьнъ (-ĭnŭ). Originally used to form adjectives from past passive participles in Old Church Slavonic, later reinterpreted as a past passive participle suffix within the Russian literary language. Compare the native past participle s

parole.significato: used to form past passive participles from verbs in -їти (-jity) and -яти (-jaty), which are frequently lexicalized int…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic -еньнъ (-enĭnŭ), from енъ (enŭ) + -ьнъ (-ĭnŭ). Originally used to form adjectives from past passive participles in Old Church Slavonic, later reinterpreted as a past passive participle suffix within the Russian literary language. Compare the native past participle s
Inherited from Old Ruthenian адъ (ad), from Old East Slavic адъ (adŭ), from Old Church Slavonic адъ (adŭ), from Ancient Greek ᾍδης (Hāídēs). Doublet of Аї́д (Ajíd).

parole.significato: alphabet (an ordered set of letters used in a language), especially the old Cyrillic alphabet.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic азъбукꙑ (azŭbuky); borrowed from Old Church Slavonic азъбоукꙑ (azŭbuky), from the names of the first two letters of the Cyrillic alphabet, азъ (azŭ) + боукꙑ (buky), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos). Attested 1627, compare язъбука (jazʺbuka) (17–18th cen
Inherited from Old Ruthenian антихристъ (antixrist), from Old East Slavic антихристъ (antixristŭ), from Old Church Slavonic антихрьстъ (antixrĭstŭ), from Koine Greek ἀντίχριστος (antíkhristos).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian апостолъ (apostol), from Old East Slavic апостолъ (apostolŭ), from Old Church Slavonic апостолъ (apostolŭ), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓πόστολος (ăpóstolos), from ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “I send off”), from ἀπό- (apó-, “from”) and στέλλω (stéllō, “I set”).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian апостольский (apostolʹskij), апостолский (apostolskij), from Old East Slavic апостольскыи (apostolĭskyi), from Old Church Slavonic апостольскъ (apostolĭskŭ). By surface analysis, апо́стол (apóstol) + -ський (-sʹkyj). Compare Russian апо́стольский (apóstolʹskij), Belarusi
From Old Church Slavonic арханг҄елъ (arxangʹjelŭ), and Ancient Greek ἀρχᾰ́γγελος (arkhắngelos).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian беззаконие (bezzakonje), from Old East Slavic беззакониѥ (bezzakonije), probably from Old Church Slavonic безакониѥ (bezakonije), itself likely a calque of Koine Greek ἀνομία (anomía). By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + зако́н (zakón) + -я (-ja). Compare Russian беззако́
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благъ (blagŭ). For sense development, compare Russian блаже́нный (blažénnyj, “fool”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоговѣйный (blagogovějnyj). Compare Russian благогове́йный (blagogovéjnyj).

parole.significato: to revere, to venerate, to be in awe of (+ пе́ред + instrumental)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благоговѣти (blagogověti). Compare Russian благогове́ть (blagogovétʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодать (blagodatĭ). By surface analysis, бла́го (bláho) + -о- (-o-) + да́ти (dáty) + -ь (-ʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благодѣѣньѥ (blagodějěnĭje). By surface analysis, благо (blaho) + -о- (-o-) + дія́ння (dijánnja)

parole.significato: well-being, prosperity, welfare (state of health, happiness and/or prosperity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благополоучиѥ (blagopolučije). By surface analysis, благо- (blaho-) + полу́чити (polúčyty) + -я (-ja). Compare Russian благополу́чие (blagopolúčije).

parole.significato: verbal noun of благословля́ти impf (blahoslovljáty) and благослови́ти pf or impf (blahoslovýty):
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благословениѥ (blagoslovenije). By surface analysis, благослови́ти (blahoslovýty) + -е́ння (-énnja). Compare Russian благослове́ние (blagoslovénije), Belarusian благаславе́нне (blahaslavjénnje).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благословити (blagosloviti), a calque of Ancient Greek ἐυλογεῖν (eulogeîn). By surface analysis, бла́го (bláho, “good”) + сло́во (slóvo, “word”) + -и́ти (-ýty). Compare Russian благослови́ть (blagoslovítʹ), Belarusian благаславі́ць (blahaslavícʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благостꙑни (blagostyni).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic благочьстивъ (blagočĭstivŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek εὐσεβής (eusebḗs). By surface analysis, благо- (blaho-) + чести́ти (čestýty) + -и́вий (-ývyj).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian блаженный (blažennyj), from Old East Slavic блаженыи (blaženyi), probably from Old Church Slavonic блаженъ (blaženŭ), passive participle of блажити (blažiti). Compare Russian блаже́нный (blažénnyj), Belarusian блажэ́нны (blažénny).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic блаженьство (blaženĭstvo). By surface analysis, блаже́нний (blažénnyj) + -ство (-stvo).
Learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic Богослꙋженіе (Bogosluženije), бог (boh) + -о- (-o-) + служити (služyty) + -і́ння (-ínnja).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic божьство (božĭstvo), a calque of Ancient Greek θεότης (theótēs). By surface analysis, бог (boh, “god”) + -ество́ (-estvó).
Inherited from Old East Slavic боꙗринъ (bojarinŭ), from Old Church Slavonic болꙗринъ (boljarinŭ).

parole.significato: demoniac, demon-possessed, devil-ridden, possessed by demons
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian бѣсноватый (běsnovatyj) (since XV), from бѣсный (běsnyj) + -оватый (-ovatyj), from Old Church Slavonic бѣсьнъ (běsĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *běsьnъ. By surface analysis, біс (bis) + -н (-n) + -ува́тий (-uvátyj).
From в'язати (vʺjazaty), Old Church Slavonic вѩзати, ⰲⱗⰸⰰⱅⰻ (vjęzati, ⰲⱗⰸⰰⱅⰻ, literally “to bind, to tie”), with -ь (-ʹ).
From Old East Slavic вельможа (velĭmoža), Old Church Slavonic вельможа (velĭmoža).

parole.significato: chains, fetters (worn by ascetics as an act of penance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic веригꙑ (verigy), the plural of верига (veriga), from Proto-Slavic *veriga.

parole.significato: to disgorge, to erupt, to eject, to belch, to spew
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian вывергнꙋти (vyverhnuti), probably a calque from Old Church Slavonic извръгнѫти (izvrŭgnǫti). By surface analysis, ви- (vy-) + ве́ргнути (vérhnuty).

An early borrowing from Old Church Slavonic виноградъ (vinogradŭ), likely during Old East Slavic [Term?] based on cognates in Russian and Belarusian вінаград (vinahrad). The two halves of the word are cognate to вино (vyno) and город (horod), with the spelling of the second element -град, marking it
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въкоупѣ (vŭkupě). By surface analysis, в (v) + ку́пі (kúpi, “bunch”).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic владꙑка (vladyka), itself derived from Old Church Slavonic владѣти (vladěti), from Proto-Slavic *volděti (“to expand”). By surface analysis, влада (vlada) + -ика (-yka).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic власть (vlastĭ). Doublet of во́лость (vólostʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вождь (voždĭ), from Proto-Slavic *voďь. Displaced inherited Old East Slavic вожь (vožĭ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic влъхвъ (vlŭxvŭ), from Old Church Slavonic влъснѫти (vlŭsnǫti, “to stutter”), referring to the trances the priests used in their ceremonies.

parole.significato: to rise from the dead, to resurrect, to revive
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въскрьсати (vŭskrĭsati), from Proto-Slavic *vъzkrьsati.

parole.significato: to raise from the dead, to resurrect, to revive
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въскрѣсити (vŭskrěsiti), from Proto-Slavic *vъzkrěsiti.

parole.significato: to rise from the dead, to resurrect, to revive
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въскрьснѫти (vŭskrĭsnǫti), from Proto-Slavic *vъzkrьsnǫti.

parole.significato: to raise from the dead, to resurrect, to revive
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въскрѣшати (vŭskrěšati), from Proto-Slavic *vъzkrěšati.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врагъ (vragŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vorgъ. Compare the inherited doublet во́рог (vóroh, “enemy, foe”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣмѧ (vrěmę). Doublet of вере́м'я (verémʺja), the inherited form.
From Old Church Slavonic олътарь (olŭtarĭ), ultimately from Latin altāre. Compare Romanian oltar, Russian алта́рь (altárʹ), dialectal волтарь (voltarʹ), Serbo-Croatian о̀лта̄р, Slovene oltár.

parole.significato: to impart, to enunciate, to proclaim
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣщати (věštati), from Proto-Slavic *věťati.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian глава́ (hlavá), from Old East Slavic глава (glava), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глава (glava). Doublet of голова́ (holová), the native East Slavic term.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic глаголъ (glagolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *golgolъ (“speech, word”).

parole.significato: to fast and attend church services in preparation for communion
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic говѣти (gověti), from Proto-Slavic *gověti.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian грекъ (hrek), from Old East Slavic грькъ (grĭkŭ), from Old Church Slavonic грькъ (grĭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *grьkъ. By surface analysis, back-formation from гре́цький (hrécʹkyj).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian грецкїй (hreckij), from Old East Slavic грьчьскъ (grĭčĭskŭ), from Old Church Slavonic грьчьскъ (grĭčĭskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *grьčьskъ.

parole.significato: to come, to begin (of time, period, event)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic грѧсти (gręsti), from Proto-Slavic *gręstì.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic доблѥсть (dobljestĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dobľestь.
From Old Church Slavonic догма (dogma), from Latin dogma, from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma), from δοκέω (dokéō).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic достоиновѣрьнъ (dostoinověrĭnŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀξιόπιστος (axiópistos). By surface analysis, досто- (dosto-) + ві́рний (vírnyj). Compare вірогі́дний (virohídnyj).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian елефа́нтъ (elefánt), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic е҆лефа́нтъ (elefántŭ), е҆лефа́нтесъ (elefántesŭ, “elephant”), further borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās) (nominative plural ελέφαντες (eléphantes)). Cognate with Ukrainian верблю́д (verbljúd), Russian вербл

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жрьтва (žrĭtva), from Proto-Slavic *žьrtva (“sacrifice”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *girʔ-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrH-. By surface analysis, Old Church Slavonic: жрьти (žrĭti) (Old Church Slavonic: žrʹty (žrĭti)) + -тва (-tva).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic житиѥ (žitije, “life”), from Proto-Slavic *žitьje, from Proto-Slavic *žiti (“to live”). Doublet of життя́ (žyttjá), the inherited East Slavic form.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic законоположеньѥ (zakonopoloženĭje). By surface analysis, зако́н (zakón) + -о- (-o-) + положи́ти (položýty) + -ення (-ennja).

parole.significato: to lock away, to imprison, to confine, to incarcerate
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic заточити (zatočiti, “to send away, to exile, to banish”), possibly via Russian заточи́ть (zatočítʹ). By surface analysis, за- (za-) + точи́ти (točýty, “to cause to run”).
From Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian злакъ (zlak), from Old East Slavic злакъ (zlakŭ), from Old Church Slavonic злакъ (zlakŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zolkъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic злато (zlato), from Proto-Slavic *zolto, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-. Doublet of зо́лото (zóloto) and зло́то (zlóto).

parole.significato: to abuse, to brutalize, to maltreat, to mistreat (to treat badly, roughly, cruelly)
parole.testo: Probably from з- (z-) + Old East Slavic гнушатися (gnušatisja), from Old Church Slavonic гнѫшати сѧ (gnǫšati sę), from Proto-Slavic *gnušati (see also *gnusъ, *gnǫsъ). Compare Russian гнуша́ться (gnušátʹsja).

parole.significato: canon (religious law or body of law decreed by a church)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic канонъ (kanonŭ), from Old Church Slavonic канонъ (kanonŭ), from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic капище (kapište, “idol; pagan temple”), from капь (kapĭ, “image”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic каѳисма (kaθisma), from Byzantine Greek κάθισμα (káthisma).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian кедръ (kedr), from Old Church Slavonic кедръ (kedrŭ), from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros).

parole.significato: Caesar (title of a Roman or Byzantine emperor)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic кесар (kesar), from Koine Greek Καῖσαρ (Kaîsar), itself a borrowing from Latin Caesar. Doublet of цар (car), це́зар (cézar), and це́сар (césar).
Old Church Slavonic кли́росъ (klírosŭ), then Byzantine Greek κλήρος (klḗros). Metathesis possibly through крило́ (kryló) ("side of the building").

Inherited from Old East Slavic лицемѣръ (liceměrŭ), from Old Church Slavonic лицемѣръ (liceměrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *liceměrъ, from Proto-Slavic *lice and *-měnъ (by surface analysis, лице́ (lycé, “face”) + міня́ти (minjáty, “to change”)). Compare Russian лицеме́р (licemér).

Inherited from Old East Slavic лицемѣрити (liceměriti), from Old Church Slavonic лицемѣрити (liceměriti). Compare Russian лицеме́рить (liceméritʹ). Can also be analysed as лицо́ (lycó, “face”) + -е- (-e-) + мі́ряти (mírjaty, “measure”)
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic маслина (maslina). By surface analysis, ма́сло (máslo) + -и́на (-ýna).

Inherited from Old East Slavic месия (mesija), from Old Church Slavonic месиꙗ (mesija), from Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic ܡܫܺܝܚܳܐ (məšīḥā), from Biblical Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšîaḥ, “anointed”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic милосьрдъ (milosĭrdŭ), from Old Church Slavonic милосрьдъ (milosrĭdŭ). By surface analysis, ми́лий (mýlyj, “kind”) + -о- (-o-) + се́рдце (sérdce, “heart”) + -ий (-yj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic миротворьць (mirotvorĭcĭ), from Old Church Slavonic. By surface analysis, мир (myr, “peace”) + -о- (-o-) + твори́ти (tvorýty, “to create”) + -е́ць (-écʹ).

parole.significato: wish for longevity, many years (of prosperity, health, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic мъногаꙗ лѣта (mŭnogaja lěta), the adjective form being the neuter plural. See the Wikipedia article for more.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian монахъ (monax), from Old Church Slavonic монахъ (monaxŭ), from Ancient Greek μοναχός (monakhós).

parole.significato: relics (a part of the body of a saint)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic мощи (mošti), plural of мошть (moštĭ), from Proto-Slavic *mȍťь. Doublet of міць (micʹ) and міч (mič).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic насѫщьнъ (nasǫštĭnŭ), a calque of Ancient Greek ἐπιούσιος (epioúsios).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic начѧло (načęlo), from Proto-Slavic *načędlo.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic начѧльникъ (načęlĭnikŭ). Also analyzable as нача́ло (načálo) + -ник (-nyk). Cognate with Czech náčelník, Polish naczelnik, Russian начальник (načalʹnik) and Serbo-Croatian načelnik.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic нєвѣгласъ (nevěglasŭ), from Proto-Slavic *nevěgolsъ.

parole.significato: need, neediness, indigence, privation, want (lack of means of subsistence)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ноужда (nužda), from Proto-Slavic *nuďa. Displaced the inherited East Slavic form ну́жа (núža). Doublet of ну́жа (núža, “lice; flies”) (obsolete).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic область (oblastĭ), from Proto-Slavic *obolstь. Displaced native Old East Slavic оболость (obolostĭ).

parole.significato: collective society (primitive, often clan-based, society with collective ownership of the means of production)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian общи́на (obščína), from Old East Slavic обьщина (obĭščina), from Old Church Slavonic обьщина (obĭština), from Proto-Slavic *obьťina.

Inherited from Old East Slavic отъкръвениѥ (otŭkrŭvenije), from Old Church Slavonic отъкръвениѥ (otŭkrŭvenije, “revelation”), from отъкрꙑти (otŭkryti, “to uncover, to reveal, to open”). Doublet of відкриття́ (vidkryttjá). Compare Russian открове́ние (otkrovénije).

parole.significato: ablution (the act of washing or cleansing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic омъвеньѥ (omŭvenĭje). By surface analysis, оми́ти (omýty) + -іння (-innja).

parole.significato: remnants, remains, debris, leftovers (the parts left over after other parts have been removed, used, or destroyed)
parole.testo: The plural of оста́нок (ostánok) (archaic), from Old Church Slavonic останъкъ (ostanŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ostanъkъ.
From Old Church Slavonic патріархъ (patriarxŭ), from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs). Compare Russian патриа́рх (patriárx), Belarusian патрыя́рх (patryjárx).

parole.significato: lamentable, deplorable, tragic, miserable, pitiful, regrettable
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плачевьнъ (plačevĭnŭ). By surface analysis, плач (plač) + -ев(ий) (-ev(yj)) + -ний (-nyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic поборьникъ (poborĭnikŭ), from поборати (poborati, “to help in a struggle, to protect”), from борь (borĭ, “struggle”).

parole.significato: to knock down, to topple, to fell, to bring down, to floor (to make someone or something fall)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic повръгнѫти (povrŭgnǫti). By surface analysis, по- (po-) + ве́ргнути (vérhnuty).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подвигъ (podvigŭ), a deverbal of подвигнѫти (podvignǫti)).

parole.significato: patron, protector, defender, custodian (one who protects or supports)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic покръвител҄ь (pokrŭvitelʹĭ), from покрꙑти (pokryti, “to protect”) + -тел҄ь (-telʹĭ, “-er”). By surface analysis, покров- (pokrov-) + -итель (-ytelʹ).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian потрѣбный, потребный (potrěbnyj, potrebnyj), from Old Church Slavonic потрѣбьнъ (potrěbĭnŭ) and Old East Slavic потрѣбный (potrěbnyj) (from Old Church Slavonic), possibly later reinforced by Old Polish potrzebny. By surface analysis, потре́ба (potréba) + -ний (-nyj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic православьнъ (pravoslavĭnŭ), in turn a calque of Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos). By surface analysis, пра́вий (právyj) + -о- (-o-) + сла́ва (sláva) + -ний (-nyj).

parole.significato: justice (the civil power dealing with law)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic правосѫдиѥ (pravosǫdije). By surface analysis, пра́вий (právyj) + -о- (-o-) + суд (sud) + -я (-ja). Compare Russian правосу́дие (pravosúdije), Belarusian правасу́ддзе (pravasúddzje), Bulgarian правосъ́дие (pravosắdie).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прапоръ (praporŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porporъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прахъ (praxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *porxъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pers-. Doublet of по́рох (pórox), the inherited East Slavic form.

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъкъ (prědŭkŭ), compare Russian предок (predok), Belarusian продак (pródak); from Proto-Slavic *perdъkъ, compare Macedonian предок (predok), Slovene prednik, Serbo-Croatian предак, Czech předek, Polish przodek. By surface analysis, пред (pred) + -ок (-ok).

parole.significato: to introduce, to present (cause (someone) to be acquainted; bring into the presence of others)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣдъставлꙗти (prědŭstavljati). By surface analysis, представл- (predstavl-) + -я́ти (-játy). Compare Russian представля́ть (predstavljátʹ), Belarusian прадстаўля́ць (pradstawljácʹ), Polish przedstawiać.

parole.significato: due to, thanks to, because of
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic прѣзъ (prězŭ), possibly reinforced by Polish przez.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣподобьнъ (prěpodobĭnŭ). Compare Russian преподо́бный (prepodóbnyj), Belarusian прападо́бны (prapadóbny).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прѣстолъ (prěstolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *perstolъ.

Possibly derived from Old Church Slavonic прѣчистъ (prěčistŭ). By surface analysis, пре- (pre-) + чи́стий (čýstyj). Compare Russian пречистый (prečistyj), Bulgarian пречист (prečist), Macedonian пречисти (prečisti).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пришьстьѥ (prišĭstĭje). Compare Belarusian прышэ́сце (pryšéscje), Bulgarian and Russian прише́ствие, Macedonian пришествие (prišestvie), Old East Slavic пришьствиѥ (prišĭstvije).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian *провидѣнье (*providěnʹje), possibly from Old Church Slavonic провидѣниѥ, провѣдѣниѥ (providěnije, prověděnije). By surface analysis, прови́діти (provýdity) + -іння (-innja).
Inherited from Old East Slavic проказа (prokaza, “leprosy”), from Old Church Slavonic проказа (prokaza, “leprosy”), from Proto-Slavic *prokaza.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прологъ (prologŭ), from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пророкъ (prorokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *prorokъ.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic псалъмъ (psalŭmŭ), from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós). Doublet of пса́льма (psálʹma).
From Old Ruthenian псалтыр (psaltyr), from Old East Slavic псалътꙑрь (psalŭtyrĭ), from Old Church Slavonic псалътꙑр҄ь (psalŭtyrʹĭ), from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic попъ (popŭ).
From Old Church Slavonic рабъ (rabŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orbъ. Doublet of роб (rob).
From Old Church Slavonic раба (raba). Doublet of ро́ба (róba, “hardworking woman”). Reanalyze as раб (rab) + -а (-a).

parole.significato: crucifix (an ornamental or symbolic sculptural representation of Christ on a cross)
parole.testo: Possibly from Old Church Slavonic распѧтиѥ (raspętije). Compare Russian распя́тие (raspjátije), Belarusian распя́цце (raspjáccje). Can be analysed as роз- (roz-) + п'ясти́ (pʺjastý, “to stretch”) + -я (-ja).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic свѧщеньнъ (svęštenĭnŭ). Compare Russian свяще́нный (svjaščénnyj), Belarusian свяшчэ́нны (svjaščénny). Doublet of свя́че́ний (svjáčényj), the inherited Old East Slavic form.

Learned borrowing from Old Church Slavonic серафимъ (serafimŭ), from Koine Greek σεραφείμ (serapheím), from Biblical Hebrew שְׂרָפִים (śərāp̄îm), the plural form of שָׂרָף (śārāp̄), often translated as "fiery ones", although meaning is uncertain; perhaps related to the root שרף (“to burn”).
From Old Church Slavonic сѵнаго́га (sünagóga), from Ancient Greek σῠνᾰγωγή (sŭnăgōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврьна (skvrĭna), from Proto-Slavic *skvьrna. Related to Czech skvrna, Slovak škvrna.

parole.significato: vile, foul, filthy, nasty, bad, obscene
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скврьнъ (skvrĭnŭ). By surface analysis, скве́рна (skvérna) + -ний (-nyj).

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скꙑтати сѧ (skytati sę), from Proto-Slavic *skytati (sę). Cognate with Russian скита́ться (skitátʹsja), Bulgarian ски́там се (skítam se), Serbo-Croatian скитати, Slovene skítati sе. More distantly cognate with Lithuanian kutė́ti (“to shake”), Proto-Germanic *skundij

parole.significato: tablet, table, stele (a slab of clay, stone or wood containing (usually religious) inscriptions)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic скрижаль (skrižalĭ), which is probably borrowed from Old Church Slavonic скрижаль (skrižalĭ).
From Old Church Slavonic [Term?].
Inherited from Old East Slavic змирна (zmirna), from Old Church Slavonic змѵрьна (zmürĭna), from Ancient Greek σμύρνα (smúrna).

parole.significato: cathedral, home church of a bishop.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съборъ (sŭborŭ) (a calque of Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ)), from Proto-Slavic *sъborъ. Doublet of збір (zbir, “assembly, gathering”), an inherited form.

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian соборныи (sobornyj), from Old East Slavic съборьныи (sŭborĭnyi), possibly borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съборьнъ (sŭborĭnŭ) along with съборъ (sŭborŭ) (whence собо́р). By surface analysis, собо́р (sobór) + -ний (-nyj). Doublet of збі́рний (zbírnyj). Compare Russia

parole.significato: conscience (moral sense of right and wrong)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣсть (sŭvěstĭ).

parole.significato: host, myriad, multitude, crowd, swarm (a large number of people or things)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съньмъ (sŭnĭmŭ), whence also Old Ruthenian сонмъ (sonm) and Old East Slavic съньмъ (sŭnĭmŭ), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sъnьmъ. Compare сойм, сейм (sojm, sejm)

parole.significato: host, myriad, multitude, crowd, swarm (a large number of people or things)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съньмище (sŭnĭmište), whence also Old Ruthenian сонмище (sonmišče) and Old East Slavic съньмище (sŭnĭmišče). By surface analysis, сонм (sonm) + -ище (-yšče).

parole.significato: to create, to do, to make, to produce
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътворити (sŭtvoriti). Doublet of створи́ти (stvorýty).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съпаситель (sŭpasitelĭ). By surface analysis, спас- (spas-) + -тель (-telʹ)

parole.significato: element (one of the four basic building blocks of matter in theories of ancient philosophers and alchemists: water, ear…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic стихия (stixija), from Old Church Slavonic стѵхии (stüxii) (feminine form стѵхиꙗ (stüxija)), from Ancient Greek στοιχεῖον (stoikheîon). Compare Russian стихи́я (stixíja), Belarusian стыхі́я (styxíja).

Probably from Old Church Slavonic стлъпотворѥниѥ (stlŭpotvorjenije, “building of a tower”) (in the context of the Tower of Babel), calque of Ancient Greek πυργοποιΐα (purgopoiḯa, “building of a tower”). By surface analysis, стовп (stovp, “column, pillar”) + -о- (-o-) + творі́ння (tvorínnja, “creatio
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic стражь (stražĭ), from Proto-Slavic *storžь (“guard”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *storʔg-. Doublet of сто́рож (stórož).

parole.significato: of the Passion (used only in set expressions relating to Holy Week)
parole.testo: Possibly from Old Church Slavonic страстьнъ (strastĭnŭ). By surface analysis, страсть (strastʹ) + -ни́й (-nýj). Compare Russian страстно́й (strastnój).

From an unattested form *стромиголов(у), related to строми́ти (stromýty, “to insert, stick”) and голова́ (holová, “head”). Possibly ultimately from Old Church Slavonic стрьмоглавь (strĭmoglavĭ, “head down, headfirst, headlong”), whence Russian стремгла́в (stremgláv). Compare also Belarusian стрымгал

parole.significato: court of law, trial (usually used ironically or to refer to an unfair one)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫдилище (sǫdilište). By surface analysis, суди́ти (sudýty, “to judge”) + -лище (-lyšče).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сꙑ (sy), present active participle of бꙑти (byti), from Proto-Slavic *sy, present active participle of *byti.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соуѥта (sujeta), from Proto-Slavic *sujeta, from *sujь + *-eta.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сионовъ (sionovŭ). By surface analysis, Сіо́н (Sión) + -овий (-ovyj). Compare Russian сио́новый (siónovyj).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тать (tatĭ), from Proto-Slavic *tatь (“thief”).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic татьба (tatĭba). By surface analysis, тать (tatʹ) + -ьба (-ʹba).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тельць (telĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *telьcь. Compare Russian and Bulgarian теле́ц (teléc), Belarusian цяле́ц (cjaljéc), Polish cielec.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тръжьство (trŭžĭstvo). By surface analysis, торг (torh) + -ество (-estvo).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣба (trěba, “rite, ceremony, necessity”), from Proto-Slavic *terba. Displaced the Old East Slavic inherited form тереба (tereba).

parole.significato: "In the Jordan river", the traditional response to a greeting on Epiphany
parole.testo: From Old Church Slavonic [Term?]
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian убїиство (ubyystvo), probably from Old Church Slavonic оубииство (ubiistvo). By surface analysis, убив- (ubyv-) + -ство (-stvo). Compare Russian уби́йство (ubíjstvo).

parole.significato: to kill (to extinguish the life of)
parole.testo: Probably from Old Church Slavonic оумрътвити (umrŭtviti). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + ме́ртвий (mértvyj) + -и́ти (-ýty). Compare Belarusian умярцві́ць (umjarcvícʹ), Russian умертви́ть (umertvítʹ).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic храмъ (xramŭ) via Old East Slavic храмъ (xramŭ). Doublet of хоро́м (xoróm) from хоромъ (xoromŭ). For sense as patrons saint's day, compare Romanian hram.
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic хранитель (xranitelĭ). By surface analysis, (obsolete, literary) храни́ти (xranýty) + -тель (-telʹ). Doublet of хорони́тель (xoronýtelʹ).
From Old Church Slavonic [Term?].
From Old Church Slavonic [Term?], compare Serbo-Croatian Христос се роди. The greeting is a quotation from St. Cosmas' Canon for the Nativity.
From Old Church Slavonic [Term?], compare Serbo-Croatian Христос се роди.
From Old Church Slavonic [Term?]
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic члѣнъ (člěnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čelnъ.
Derived from Old Church Slavonic чьсти (čĭsti) / читати (čitati, “to read, to count”). Cognate with Russian чёткий (čótkij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic юнъ (junŭ), from Proto-Slavic *junъ.

parole.significato: pagan, heathen (not adhering to an Abrahamic religion)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ꙗзычникъ (jazyčnik), from Old East Slavic ѧзꙑчьникъ (języčĭnikŭ), from Old Church Slavonic ѩзꙑчьникъ (języčĭnikŭ), a calque of Byzantine Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós). By surface analysis, (archaic) язи́к (jazýk, “ethnos”) + -ник (-nyk).
Derived from Old Church Slavonic ѥдинъ (jedinŭ) + -ий (-yj). Related to Ukrainian оди́н (odýn).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic єпархиꙗ (eparxija), borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπαρχία (eparkhía).

parole.significato: letter "ъ", now called тверди́й знак (tverdýj znak)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѥръ (jerŭ).

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian єресь (jeresʹ), from Old East Slavic ѥресь (jeresĭ), from Old Church Slavonic ѥресь (jeresĭ), from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis). Compare Russian е́ресь (jéresʹ), Belarusian е́рась (jérasʹ).

parole.significato: letter "ь", now called м'яки́й знак (mʺjakýj znak)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ѥрь (jerĭ).

parole.significato: echidna (any of the species of small spined monotremes in the family Tachyglossidae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian єхидна (jexydna, “venomous snake”), from Old East Slavic ехидьна (jexidĭna, “venomous snake”), from Old Church Slavonic ѥхидьна (jexidĭna), from Ancient Greek ἔχιδνα (ékhidna, “viper, snake”).
From Old East Slavic ігу́мен (igúmen), from Old Church Slavonic игоумєнъ (igumenŭ), from Byzantine Greek ἡγούμενος (hēgoúmenos).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic икона (ikona), from Greek εικόνα (eikóna), from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic истина (istina), from Proto-Slavic *jьstina. By surface analysis, (archaic) і́стий (ístyj) + -ина (-yna). Compare Latvian īstens (“real, true, genuine”).
